sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for colu1241 (Columbia-Wenatchi / Moses-Columbia Salish, catalog classification lexical): the Glottolog entry 'Zimmermann, Hucklebridge & Nelson 2018b' (NELS 48, pp. 275-284) is actually single-authored by Eva Zimmermann (Hucklebridge & Nelson edited the volume; confirmed on the author's publications page). downloaded the open pre-publication draft from evazimmermann.org (14 pp. It is a Gradient Harmonic Grammar reanalysis using Czaykowska-Higgins' and Willett's data, not first-hand fieldwork. Sec. 2 states: one main stress per word; default on the rightmost underlying vowel, default-to-opposite (initial epenthetic vowel) when no underlying vowel; prefixes never stressed; placement otherwise decided by a six-class lexical competition (D* > SE/WE ~ D > S > R* > R > W) with a locality threshold; rightmost among same-type suffixes; optional secondary stress on surviving pretonic suffix vowels (sec. 3.3). This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding — indeed the catalog's deciding quote already cites this draft (sec. 2) verbatim and links its URL, so 'already_listed=false' is a bibliography-listing gap, not a reading gap. Nothing new to acquire; the paper does not supersede the Czaykowska-Higgins 1985 primary (the fuller first-hand source it relies on, Czaykowska-Higgins 1993a NLLT 11:197-278, DOI 10.1007/BF00992914, is paywalled and already in the catalog's links). direct download of the author's site was used instead.

This is exactly the catalog's 'lexical' coding and its the primary-stress rule text; the paper is a secondary theoretical restatement built on Czaykowska-Higgins' data (1985, 1993a NLLT, 2011) and Willett 2003.

sources.citation: Willett, Marie Louise. 2003. A Grammatical Sketch of Nxa'amxcin (Moses-Columbia Salish). PhD dissertation, University of Victoria. xii+464 pp. (via the Internet Archive of UVicSpace bitstream; live DSpace could not be reached by automated download)
sources.quote: 'The highly complex stress system in Nxaʔamxcín is elaborately discussed in Czaykowska-Higgins (1993a) ... [quoting Cz-H p.198] "[i]n all the Interior Salish languages the position of primary stress is affected by idiosyncratic morphological stress properties". Czaykowska-Higgins recognizes two major classes of roots ... strong and weak, the former containing a full vowel ... the latter a schwa. The two classes of suffixes are referred to as dominant and recessive. Dominant suffixes trigger stress shift to the right, while recessive suffixes may or may not, depending on the class of the root.
sources.note: Only reference grammar (Glottolog's sole 'grammar' entry); sec. 4.5 summarizes 1993a and confirms lexical accent + rightmost-full-vowel default. now obtained.
